depth: The depth map shows a broad exterior walkway bordered by multi-storey building walls on the left (~3–6 m) and right (~3–8 m). Its ground forms a smooth bright-to-dark gradient, extending from 1 m in the lower foreground to beyond 15 m in the dark background. A low bollard light on the path’s left side is ~4–5 m ahead in frame 1 and closes to ~1.5 m at the extreme left edge by frame 5, where it is partly cropped from view. A pedestrian, facing away, is slightly right of the bollard and ~2–4 m farther forward, placing them ~5–9 m from the camera wearer. In frame 3, the wearer’s extended left arm is clearly outlined in the lower-left foreground at <0.5 m, within arm’s reach, and blocks part of the mid-ground pavement; this boundary is far less visible in the dark RGB image. Through the five frames, greater brightness in the bollard, building pillars, and pedestrian silhouette reflects the wearer’s steady forward motion and slight pan to the right after lowering the arm in frame 4. Still, the map is unreliable: frame 2 entirely omits the raised, dark-sleeved arm; frame 3’s motion blur causes the pedestrian and farther bollard to disappear into the dark background; and the distant courtyard archway (>15 m) is compressed into uniform black.
segmentation: The instance-segmentation output remains largely empty throughout the dark nighttime scene: masks appear only in frames 1 and 4, whereas frames 2, 3, and 5 are entirely blank. In frame 1, the system labels the pedestrian walking away on the left, ~8–9 m from the camera wearer, as a 'person'. It incorrectly labels the nearer illuminated bollard, ~4–5 m away and ~3–4 m ahead of and left of the pedestrian, as a second 'person'. When the camera wearer draws closer in frame 4, the pedestrian is again segmented as a 'person' at ~5–6 m ahead, facing away and not looking toward the wearer; this helps separate the silhouette from the dim background where RGB contrast is weak. Yet frame 4 also wrongly identifies the nearer left-side bollard, ~2.5–3 m ahead, as a 'parking meter', and classifies the farther bollard light immediately left of the pedestrian’s legs, ~6 m away and partly hidden by the pedestrian, as another small 'person'. Overall, the map is highly unreliable: it misses the pedestrian completely in frames 2, 3, and 5, does not detect the camera wearer’s extended arm and hand in frames 2 and 3 (<0.5 m and the sole object within arm’s reach), and supplies no segmentation for the walkway or surrounding buildings.
pose: Every one of the five pose frames is entirely black, with neither yellow body skeletons nor magenta hand skeletons rendered. The RGB sequence nevertheless shows a pedestrian on the walkway’s left side in all five frames, ~5–9 m ahead, moving away with their back facing the camera wearer. The wearer’s own left arm and hand project forward into the lower-left portion of the view in frames 2 and 3 at <0.5 m, within arm’s reach, before falling below the lower frame boundary in frame 4. With no keypoints detected, the pose output adds no spatial evidence beyond the RGB imagery and is unable to follow the pedestrian’s gait or facing direction, or the extension and subsequent retraction of the camera wearer’s arm. This complete failure demonstrates how unreliable body and hand pose estimation is under dim nighttime illumination, severe motion blur in frames 2 and 3, and the pedestrian’s medium-to-far viewing distances of >5 m.
